01.r: Turns the speech to a new audience: the Levites.
01.n: The phrase stands first in the Hebrew, 'and to the Levites you shall speak', which puts the weight on who is being addressed.

02.r: The members of the tribe of Levi who serve at the sanctuary.
02.n: BDB notes that the plural is always a noun, 'Levites', the tribe as a class of servants.

03.r: Moses is told to pass the instruction on.
03.n: The verb is imperfect, 'you shall speak', used as a command; most translations make it a plain imperative, 'speak'. The 'you' is singular: Moses.

04.r: Introduces the words Moses is to say.
04.n: A perfect with 'and', which carries on the command of the verb before it. YLT renders the perfect form literally, 'thou hast said'.

06.r: Sets the occasion: when the tithe comes into the Levites' hands.

07.r: The Levites receive the people's tithe.
07.n: The 'you' is now plural: the Levites as a body. The verb is the ordinary one for taking, as wide as English 'take'; the DRC and BSB read it as 'receive'.

08.r: Marks the people the tithe comes from.
08.n: Literally 'from with': two prepositions joined. BDB lists this pair under the word 'with' as meaning 'from', from proximity.

09.r: The descendants of Israel: the whole people.
09.n: Literally 'sons'. The BSB folds 'sons of Israel' into one word, 'the Israelites'.

10.r: The nation named after its ancestor Jacob.
10.n: BDB gives Israel as the second name of Jacob, and the name of the Hebrew nation.

11.r: Marks 'the tithe' as the object of 'take'.
11.n: This small word marks a definite direct object and has no English equivalent; it is counted here with 'the tithe'.

12.r: The tenth of produce that the people give.
12.n: The Hebrew is singular, 'the tithe'; the KJV, Geneva and DRC make it plural. Gesenius derives the word from the noun for 'ten'.

13.r: Introduces what God says about the tithe.

14.r: God himself has handed the tithe to the Levites.
14.n: A perfect: the gift is already made and stands.

16.n: Again 'from with them', the same pair of prepositions as before 'the sons of Israel'. The DRC and BSB leave it out.

17.r: The tithe takes the place, for the Levites, of a share of land.
17.n: Literally 'in your inheritance'; the preposition here marks what the tithe counts as, so 'as' or 'for'. Gesenius gives possession, domain, and cites Numbers 18:21 for this sense; that verse is in the same passage.

18.r: The Levites are to lift a portion off the tithe they receive.
18.n: The causative form of a verb that Gesenius and BDB give as to rise, be high: so 'make high, lift up'. BDB's entry also records 'take away, remove'. A perfect with 'and' after the 'when' clause, so 'then you shall'; YLT renders the perfect form literally, 'ye have lifted up'.

19.r: From the tithe the Levites have received.

20.r: The portion lifted off and set apart for the LORD.
20.n: The noun comes from the same root as the verb 'lift up' before it (Gesenius), so the Hebrew reads 'lift up from it the lifted portion'. Gesenius gives an oblation, offering, gift, especially brought to the temple and the priests; BDB lists among its uses a contribution to the LORD set apart for priests. We keep 'contribution' throughout, where older translations say 'heave offering'.

21.r: The personal name of Israel's God.
21.n: Literally 'the contribution of the LORD'; Gesenius records this exact phrase. Most translations turn it into 'for the LORD'.

22.r: The size of the Levites' contribution: one tenth.
22.n: The same word as 'the tithe' earlier in the verse, now without the article. The KJV, Geneva and DRC say 'tenth part' here, where our register keeps 'tithe'.

23.r: Marks the tithe the portion is taken from.
23.n: Gesenius records a similar phrase without this word, 'the tithe of the tithe', citing Neh. 10:39. Here the preposition 'from' is written, and every translation renders it 'of'.

24.r: The tithe the Levites received from the people.

01.n: The Greek has 'and' with the dative case, 'and to the Levites', where the Hebrew writes a preposition.

02.n: Dictionary form supplied by hand: the matched form is marked loose. Our Greek text spells the word λευείταις.

07.n: Dictionary form supplied by hand: the brief gives none. λάβητε, 'you take'.

09.n: Our Greek text reads 'from the sons', with no word for 'Israel' after it. The brief cannot show whether Swete omits it or the digital text dropped it.

12.n: ἐπιδέκατον, 'the tenth part'. The translators use this word, not δεκάτη, for each 'tithe' in this verse.

17.n: κλῆρος means a lot, and so a share assigned by lot: 'in your lot' for 'in your inheritance'.

18.n: Our Greek text has only 'and you' here, with no verb for 'lift up'. A verb has likely been lost in the digital text; that is an inference, not something the brief shows.

20.n: ἀφαίρεμα, 'something taken off': the Greek picks up the 'take away, remove' side of the Hebrew verb rather than 'lift up'.

21.n: κυρίῳ, 'to the Lord': the Greek turns 'the contribution of the LORD' into 'a portion for the Lord'.

24.n: Printed ἐπικαὶ in our Greek text: evidently a garbled ἐπιδεκάτου, 'the tenth part', which is what the matched dictionary form gives.
